newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin works on U.S. summit after govt reshuffle.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin works on U.S. summit after govt reshuffle.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin retreated to a country residence on Tuesday to turn his attention to a summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton after plotting Russia's deepest government reshuffle in five years.

Presidential spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin had gone to the Gorky-9 residence outside Moscow to prepare for the summit on Thursday and Friday in Helsinki and his only planned meeting was with Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.

Primakov briefed Yeltsin on three days of pre-summit talks in Washington which left Russia and the United States divided on NATO's eastward expansion plans, although he signalled that Moscow wanted an accommodation with Washington.

"Russia understands that NATO is a real force, and Russia wants to have normal relations with NATO, which would serve the cause of normalising the situation in Europe," Primakov told reporters in Washington after talks with Clinton.
The Kremlin press service gave little detail of the Yeltsin-Primakov meeting.

Yeltsin, 66, has taken a tough stance before the summit, ruling out concessions and criticising U.S. policy towards Russia. But he has also made clear he is determined to prevent a return to Cold War tensions.
The summit will be Yeltsin's first foreign trip since last April and offers him a chance to prove himself on the world stage after heart surgery on November 5.
He has already reasserted his authority after returning to the Kremlin last month following long absences caused by the heart problems and then pneumonia.
The latest act showing his restored grip on power was a reshuffle unveiled on Monday, bringing a new young team of reformists into the cabinet.

"The president hopes that the new government -- a united and to great extent renewed team -- will jointly work on normalising the situation in the country, primarliy in the social sphere," Yastrzhembsky told Interfax news agency.
Yeltsin appointed Boris Nemtsov, 37, a leading regional pro-reform governor, as first deputy prime minister and gave several other reformers the rank of deputy prime minister.

Nemtsov joins liberal reformer Anatoly Chubais, 41, as first deputy prime minister under Chernomydrin, creating a progressive team which has been handed responsibility for injecting new life into Russia's stalled economic reforms.
Chubais also takes the finance ministry portfolio in the most far-reaching cabinet changes since liberal Yegor Gaidar became post-Soviet Russia's first de-facto premier in 1991.

"The main task of the government will be broadening and speeding up the reforms in the social and economic spheres, the practical side being the top priority," Chernomyrdin said on Tuesday, presenting Chubais to the ministry's officials.
"The situation in the country has to be quickly changed to the better, and all conditions for it have been created."
Yeltsin, in televised comments to Nemtsov on Monday, said: "Two young men -- you and Anatoly Chubais -- create a fresh young team in the government -- from scratch".
Their prime task is to implement change in the face of inertia and deepening social discontent in the provinces.
Some conservative ministers lost their jobs or were demoted, although the full line-up has not been revealed.
Minister Anatoly Kulikov stayed on as deputy prime minister. Some questions lingered over Defence Minister Igor Rodionov's future but Primakov looked set to stay on.

Primakov had hoped for a breakthrough in Washington in the dispute over NATO's plans to offer membership to former Soviet allies in eastern and central Europe, although a final deal on this had never been likely in Helsinki.
Russia says such moves threaten its security and would create new divisions in Europe.
